utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Monday, the 14th of July, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Stringer and his assistants, and good afternoon to everyone assisting us, among others the interpreters. There are a number of issues that the Trial Chamber would like to deal with, administrative matters. First of all, by a motion of the 9th of July, 2008, Mr. Karnavas, the Prosecution requested the Prlic Defence to provide additional information to the 65 ter summary of Witness Borislav Puljic, who is expected to testify shortly. Before issuing its decision on this, the Trial Chamber would like to hear the submissions of the Prlic Defence. Mr. Karnavas, can you please tell us whether you intend or not to provide an additional summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. At some point, we will try to provide them with some additional information. I really don't understand what it is that they want, other than what they already have, which is basically what he is going to testify to, but we will try to provide some additional information. That said, this particular individual, who was scheduled to be the very last witness prior to our break, it would appear that it's a virtual impossibility, if we really want to do justice with -- well, I use that word loosely -- with the other witnesses because of the timing purposes. It would appear that the current witness, Mr. Buntic, is probably not going to finish until tomorrow at the earliest, perhaps, after the first session on Wednesday. We then have the following witness, Mr. Perkovic, who happens to be in town and ready to go, ready to go. But even with us going on Friday, it would appear to me that -- and if he were to go on Friday, it would take Friday and probably all day Monday to finish him. Now, already we have scheduled Mr. Zuzul for Friday and Monday. If you may recall, that was our first witness, and we were unable to complete him. It would be our proposal that at this point in time, to contact Mr. Zuzul to see whether he can be available for Tuesday of next week, to start Tuesday, and then have Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday for him, or Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday as the buffer, as opposed to starting with Mr. Perkovic, putting him on ice while we deal with Mr. Zuzul. That way, we don't want to inconvenience these people more than we are already doing so. They're cooperating. Now, the one technical problem is with Mr. Zuzul, of course, we have no means of -- well, we're forbidden to communicate with him, and so the question is: Can someone from the witness section communicate with him or, with the Court's leave, I could -- or Ms. Tomanovic, contact Mr. Zuzul strictly for the purpose of finding out whether it would be possible for him to come on Tuesday as opposed to this Friday. And so -- and if he can't, of course, then we will -- Mr. Perkovic will simply have to work around it. Mr. Perkovic does work for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He is going to stay longer than he has anticipated. Today he did contact his ministry to let them that it looks like he's going to be longer here in The Hague than was expected, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs was gracious enough to agree that he should remain here as long as necessary, within reason, of course. Needless to say, his family would like him back as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Karnavas, the best solution would be for the Victims and Witnesses Section to call Mr. Zuzul in the afternoon to ask him whether he could come to The Hague next Tuesday; that will be done this afternoon at the earliest. Afterwards, we'll complete -- or we'll add Mr. Perkovic after Mr. Zuzul. In other words, Mr. Puljic will only come and testify at the end of August. We won't be able to hear him before that, because for Mr. Zoran Perkovic, you had provided for six hours of testimony, and six hours, you know that it's about two days of hearing, at the minimum. This afternoon, the Victims and Witnesses Section is going to get in touch with Mr. Zuzul. If he tells us that he'll be here on Tuesday, then our problem is solved, because we had told him to come on Friday, but at the time we were not aware that we would be meeting with this problem. I'm sure that this provides an answer to the questions of Mr. Stringer, who wanted to deal with the scheduling of the following witnesses. Am I right, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think it does assist us in our own preparations. As we understand it, and I think the name of the witness that's appearing in the transcript is not correct. There are references to Pusic, and I think it's a different -- Puljic. So it's our understanding that Mr. Puljic will not appear until after -- sometime after the summer recess. And that being the case, I think we can set aside for the time being the sufficiency or insufficiency of the witness summary that's been provided. The Prosecution position on that is contained in our submission, and we can perhaps set that aside for now. We can then assume that Mr. Puljic will not appear, and hopefully Mr. Zuzul then will be available to be begin a cross-examination on Tuesday of next week, which we could then take the remainder of next week or -- I guess conditions would allow a full cross-examination without the pressure of having another witness come after him, and so that is acceptable as well to the Prosecution. And it also allows, I think, for the potential that Mr. Buntic may continue a little bit longer than has been previewed so far, simply because it seems that every day with him, things tend to get a little longer, drawn out. It's my understanding that the Prosecution has about seven hours or so for its cross-examination, so I think that the proposal by Mr. Karnavas is one that's acceptable, assuming in fact that Mr. Zuzul hopefully can then become -- can come to begin his cross-examination on Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, let me deal again with the summary of Mr. Borislav Puljic. There are three points that may seem a bit vague on the basis of the summary you provided. Apparently he mentioned a crisis staff in Mostar and ADA [phoen] Commission as well, and we don't quite see what this commission is. And the third point has to do with state-owned companies in the field of reconstruction. So these three items could be clarified, because they're slightly confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will do that, we will do that. And as you -- when we do provide the additional information, Mr. President, you will see that much of that is already in the evidence already. But we will provide that so that there's no misunderstanding on any of those three issues. Thank you. And I should note that he's not going to be our very first witness coming back from the break, and we do intend to provide -- we do intend to provide an updated list. So before the end of next week, everybody will know our batting order, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. I know that the Trial Chamber is aware of our position. I think it may be worth stating. Counsels' summaries are useful in that they provide a list of topics, I think, which -- that the witness can be expected to testify about. It's our position, based on the Rule and the precedent, the decisions of other Trial Chambers, that in fact more is required of a witness summary under the Rule, Rule 65, in that not only are we entitled to a summary or a list of topics, but we're also entitled to know what it is the witness is going to say. And of course that's particularly true, in our view, when there's no witness statement. And so that is our position. It's the position we've set out in our papers. But, again, we understand that Mr. Puljic will not be testifying now for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last administrative matter, to respond to the submissions made last week by Mr. Stewart. In order to respond to the submissions made by Ms. Alaburic and by Mr. Stewart, we'll read again paragraph 15 of the decision it issued on the 29th of May, 2008, clarifying the decision adopting guidelines for the presentation of Defence evidence. This is what we stated in that decision, and that should respond to the concerns expressed by Mr. Stewart. I'm going to read out this very slowly. The Chamber agrees that it is not always easy to distinguish between a subject already discussed with a witness during the examination-in-chief and a subject that could be qualified as new that was discussed for the first time during cross-examination of the witness. It might, indeed, be difficult to distinguish between the different subjects that are discussed. In order to make recording the time as clear as possible and facilitate the work of the Court Deputy, the Trial Chamber invites the cross-examining party to indicate, before the beginning of cross-examination, the subjects it would like to discuss with the witness, explaining the extent to which they were already discussed with the witness during the examination-in-chief. The Chamber will decide whether this is a new subject and deduct this time from the total time allocated for the presentation of the case of the cross-examining party. The Chamber will ask the Court Deputy to record this time according to guideline 7, paragraph 21(c) of the decision of 24 April 2008. In other words, when counsel begins his or her cross-examination, as will be the case later on with Ms. Alaburic, it's up to counsel to tell us what matters -- what subjects will be dealt with during cross-examination than that have already been dealt with during the examination-in-chief led by Mr. Karnavas. Counsel, Ms. Alaburic, will have to tell us which subjects she will deal with that have not been raised during the examination-in-chief, and for these matters time will be deducted from the time she was allocated for the presentation of her Defence case. In case of challenges or in case of what I would call borderline subjects, it will be up to the Trial Chamber to tell the Court Deputy, and of course that will be notified to the Defence, it will be up to the Chamber to tell the Court Deputy how time should be allocated. In other words, it's up to counsel to tell us at the beginning, well, the witness dealt with items A, B, C and D, and "as part of my cross-examination, I will be discussing items B, C or D, but I will also deal with a new matter, and these are E, F, G, H," and so on and so forth, and we'll understand immediately that these new items, E, F, and so on and so forth, will be deducted from the item of the cross-examining counsel. This is our response to Mr. Stewart, to give him additional information and to reassure him as for allocation of time, but in the end it's always up to the Trial Chamber to decide how time is allocated. This, I recall, is something we outlined in our decision of 29th of May, 2008, and if all Defence counsel comply with this decision, we should not have any problems. Let me now deal with the time we have left. I believe that Ms. Nozica has about 50 minutes left, 5-O, and then 4D will have one hour and 30 minutes. Ms. Nozica, good afternoon, again. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know I have another 50 minutes but according to yours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so fast that I completely forgot our witness. And she made the same mistake so let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think before the witness comes I can say this. I know I have 50 minutes. I will enumerate the subjects I want to cover with this witness, and I will ask the Trial Chamber if I apply for another 50 minutes, to allow me to have them, to be deduced from my total time. And all the subjects I'm going to be covering have been raised in direct examination. One is, to begin with, the Central Military Prison. Then I will move on to the subject of appointment of prosecutors and judges in Military Courts and Military Prosecutors Offices. After that, I will move on to the subject of reporting in the military judiciary bodies, to be followed by the subject of financing of military judiciary bodies, and then the subject of military prisons; namely, who appointed wardens and who controlled military prisons. And to end with, I would like to go very briefly with the witness through certain provisions of the law on the military criminal procedure, which should shed light on certain points that he was examined on by Mrs. Tomasegovic-Tomic, and some subjects from my cross-examination, so we shall see what the legislation at that time prescribed. I will be very economical in my use of time and will try to go very quickly through anything that might appear as repetition. But still I am in the hands of the witness, and I therefore hope that you will grant me some tolerance if the examination is a bit lengthier, because before us we have a witness who can give us information from the horse's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I hope you had a pleasant weekend, that it didn't -- it was not too long. And I'm now going to give the floor to Ms. Nozica, who will proceed with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic. I have already greeted everyone else in the courtroom. Just to remind you briefly, we have LiveNote and it's simple for us, but I need to remind you where we left off. On Thursday, we were going through documents, and we have shown how the Central Military Prison was established. We have shown that this was done in order to transfer military prisoners and prisoners of war. I will now ask you to look at a document in my binder, 1D 1976. Just tell me when you have found it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a report, then I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is a report from the Department of Justice for the period July to November, 1993. I will refer you to the last paragraph in Croatian, and that's the penultimate paragraph in English, which says: "In respect to the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor penalties, there was only the District Prison in Mostar in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna when the war began." Mr. Buntic, you have already confirmed that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the record and reliability, you have called document 1D 1976, and it's so recorded, but it seems to me that we're dealing with document 1D 1797.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both the witness and I have before us 1D -- 1D -- sorry, 1D 01976. It's a report from the military -- from the Department of Justice for July to November. If Your Honour does not have it, I can give you the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'll take the opportunity to compliment you on the way you have organised the documents here. I was still looking in the back, and there -- that's why I didn't find it. I apologise to you and at the same time thank you for having so nicely organised the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your praise is always welcome. Let us move on to the next sentence. It reads: "However, during the reporting period, the location of the prison building became the frontline and the prison could no longer serve its purpose, which is why the inmates were relocated to the Heliodrom in Mostar." Mr. Buntic, if you would first confirm what is said in the report.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The decision to establish the Central Military Prison Heliodrom was made in the beginning of September, 1992, and the civilian inmates of the Civilian District Prison in Mostar were relocated to Heliodrom sometime between the 20th and the 30th September, 1992. I'm sorry, I meant military prisoners and prisoners of war. They were transferred to Heliodrom between the 20th and 30th of September, after the Central Military Prison for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one quick question about civilian prisoners. You are a lawyer, and you will have no problem answering my question. As for civilian prisoners, did they have to be detained after a document had been issued, either a decision by a court, by an investigating magistrate, or because they had to serve a sentence? In other words, when we are talking about civilian prisoners, does it mean that there was a paper -- a document stating that they were to be detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already answered this question, in part. As we have read, the time when I assumed my position, the District Prison in Mostar was the only prison facility where all prisoners had to be held, where sentences meted out by final sentences were served by all inmates in this prison. That's in Ricina Street, just behind the building of the Higher Court in Mostar, so it was a civilian prison. I also said that as a result of the circumstances that arose as a result of the aggression and the occupation of Mostar by the Yugoslav People's Army, this prison also held prisoners of all categories, all that the former JNA had taken prisoner and later the HVO and the BH Army, that is, the independent 4th Corps. All these people were held in this prison. And I have already mentioned that through my contacts with the president of the Higher Court in Mostar, who familiarised me with the situation, I responded immediately by writing a letter to the Department of Defence, with a request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Witness. You haven't answered my question. As you can imagine, my question was very precise. We would like to know the following: When the prisoner is a civilian, does he or she have to be detained pursuant to a judicial decision? It is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was a civilian, then he could be held in that prison only based on a final judgement made by the competent court. All the other prisoners held there were held there with no legal grounds, and that is why the request was made to adapt or find other premises where that category of prisoners could be transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In case a civilian is in custody without any judicial decision, what is the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a situation where the civilian should have properly been released, and I did ask for all such persons to be released. At that time, the warden was -- just a moment. It will come back in a moment, hopefully. But the first time, and I'm talking about the period after September, the first time that the warden failed to act upon a final legal decision, the president of the Higher Court informed me the Department of Justice and General Administration started legal proceedings and relieved the warden, Pero Nikolic, I remember now, of his duties as warden, and immediately notified the civilian police thereof. I'm talking about the regimen and the procedure that prevailed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, right now, in response to the question by Judge Antonetti, you answered that within the jurisdiction of the civilian courts, civilian prisoners were those who were convicted. I'm going to ask you were there also those who were remanded in custody, against whom proceedings were underway and the judge decided they would be remanded in custody, pending judgement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two different things. One category are convicts who have been sentenced by a judgement that was rendered and made final, and the others were remanded in custody, awaiting judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So there were both convicts and those who were remanded in custody?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go one step further. Both these groups were transferred to Heliodrom. You confirmed that already. Just tell me when.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about this category, they were transferred to Heliodrom only in May 1993, after a conflict broke out between Bosniaks and Croats in Mostar. That could have been between the 10th and 15th 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Buntic, who had control or jurisdiction over those persons who had been transferred from the civilian prison, from the District Prison in Ricina to Heliodrom? Who was supposed to supervise the detention of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the period after May 1993, if we are talking about the Central Military Prison in Heliodrom, a special civilian section was set up, and that civilian section was still supervised by the warden of the civilian prison. I think it was Pero Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Pero Nikolic was a warden of a special section in Heliodrom, where civilians were held.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the next paragraph, which is very interesting. Just give us your very brief comments. Let's note first that from May 1993 onwards, Heliodrom holds prisoners of war, members of the HVO or, more precisely, persons under the jurisdiction of military judicial bodies, and civilians, that is, persons under the jurisdiction of civilian judiciary bodies; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, but I would like to add: jurisdiction over civilians who were convicted by final decision of civilian courts, or, as we have said earlier on, were in custody pursuant to investigative decisions of an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. You are talking too fast. Could you speak a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...to say, and you are also overlapping. You should make a little pause. As you are talking the same language, of course you naturally answer immediately, but it causes difficulty for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, we read: "Due to war operations and for reasons linked to other purposes of these buildings, they were anything but buildings for holding convicts and prisoners. Only through acts of self-initiative and decisions of unauthorised bodies, they were converted into penitential centres without any supervision by higher authorities."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They were turned into detention centres. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you meant by this paragraph? But please, Mr. Buntic, be very concise and brief, because I have very little time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the sentence is self-explanatory, because from what my prior evidence showed, it is well known that on these locations, in these centres or prisons, there happened to be a large number of people who were not held there on the basis of any judgement of a competent court or even a decision on remand in custody by investigating judges. I did not see any justification for that, except in the case of prisoners of war who could be held there without any final judgement for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take advantage of the break, with your permission. You have indicated, unless I misunderstood, that you were of the opinion that these prisoners, without title, should be released, but apparently they were not released. Now, who was deciding against you? You were the Minister of Justice and you said you had the ultimate authority. How come that you did not simply make an order, ministerial order, prisoners without title are to be released immediately, full stop, signed "Buntic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, you're quite right. When it comes to the civilian department of the Heliodrom Prison, I had jurisdiction over that section. I visited the civilian section of the Heliodrom Prison, and having observed certain irregularities, I did as much as I described to you. We launched disciplinary proceedings against the warden, who was subsequently removed. As for the military section of the prison, I had no jurisdiction over it whatsoever and was unable to take any measures in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, it's okay to take disciplinary proceedings against the warden. My question was a slightly different one. If someone is held without title, that's unlawful deprivation of liberty and unlawful imprisonment, and the person ought to be immediately released. You have not said that they were released, and you have not said why not. You only said that -- or I seem to have understood you that you thought they should be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following my visit to the civilian department of Heliodrom, all the persons held there without final decisions to that effect were released. There weren't many of them in that department. I believe there were only two or three. I'm referring to what happened during my visit and to what I was able to observe there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, this is also for the benefit of the Judges. There is P3350, a document in the binder, which under item 12 confirms precisely what you've just said; namely, that civilians were transferred to Heliodrom. We will not, therefore, deal with this point any longer. Let us move on to a new topic, i.e., the appointment of individuals to various judicial posts, in particular in the military judiciary body and the Supreme Court and Prosecutor's Office of the HZ-HB. I hope we shall be able to go through this quickly. You said that the Defence Department was responsible, in terms of organisation, personnel and finances, for military courts and military prosecutors' offices. On the issue of appointments, Mr. Buntic, are you able to tell us who, in addition to the head of the Defence Department, nominated military prosecutors and judges in the relevant time period, those who were able to adjudicate cases before military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the Defence Department, nominations for military judges and military prosecutors' office lay within the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice and General Administration as well. One has to distinguish between two time periods. The period following the 3 of July, 1992, decree whereby the Department of Justice and General Administration was to be responsible for that, but this one, as we said, was not applied. According to the 17th of October, 1992, decree, however, the Defence Department was supposed to do that. I said that regardless of the fact that the Defence Department was given this jurisdiction, it was the Department for Justice and General Administration which mostly nominated these individuals, because this particular department had a great deal of information on the persons eligible for military judges and military prosecutors' offices, particularly so because judges were quite in short supply at the time. For these reasons, it was the Department for Justice and General Administration that put forth most of the nominations for these posts, many more than the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic. I felt compelled to clarify this because you were shown document 1D 1898. We can see it in e-court. I haven't prepared it in the binder. This is the nomination of the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic, dated the 16th of January. This is a proposal for the HZ-HB Presidency, for the election of judges and judge-jurors in the District Court in -- since we haven't dealt with this, I -- that's why I'm asking you this question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just correct you? I think you said the candidates -- well, what it says here, it's judges and judge-jurors of the District Military Court. I believe you misspoke and said "prison" in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're right. That's quite clear now. Let's go quickly through the document -- through the documents. The first one is 1D 1179. As far as I know, you have seen all these documents, and we can only confirm that this is the period before the decree was adopted. The date is the 20th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Pages 4 of both versions are the ones where we have the nominees. You've already said, however, that these were the nominees prior to the issuance of the decree; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is P00559, P00559. You were also shown this document on direct examination, and this document predates the issuance of the decree as well, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 7th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. These were nominations accepted by the Presidency of the session of the 17th October. I believe that these were discussed at the same session of the 17th of October, when the decree was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, does the same apply to the following document, 1D 2001, that these were also proposals subsequently accepted at the meeting of the HZ-HB Presidency? The document I'm referring to you is the next one in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the proposals put forth prior to the 17th of October, 1992, were considered at the meeting of the Presidency held on the 17th of October and adopted as such. I have this one proposal for the election of the judges that was sent to the SDA in Mostar. I don't know if this is the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear, on the basis of this document, that these were -- that some of the judges for district courts were nominated by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the very documents, as well as the subsequent decisions published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Herzegovina. It follows quite clearly that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised the district military courts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that they even went on to nominate certain judges of solely Muslim ethnicity into these courts. In other words, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted that other judges of Croat ethnicity would be nominated by the relevant bodies of the HZ-HB. Judging from the names of the judges, it is quite obvious that they are Muslims. As for this document, I sent this document to the Party of Democratic Action in Mostar in order to nominate judges -- or, rather, the judges for misdemeanors in Mostar, the president of the Lower Court in Mostar and the president of the District Military Court in Mostar. My apologies, however. I believe it is necessary to add that all these discussions and contacts were the result of the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement signed in Medjugorje on the 21st of July, 1992, and my conversations with Mr. Jusuf Halilagic, who was Deputy Minister of Justice of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, this explanation you provided to us is very precious for us. However, I believe that you've already said this during the examination-in-chief. I do not want to cover ground that has already been covered. What I want is for you to confirm that this document is part of the preparatory activities for the sessions of the Presidency where a large number of prosecutors and judges were elected. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at that particular meeting of the Presidency briefly. That's page 12 of your text and page 13 of the English version. There, you propose these decrees at this fifth meeting, decrees which have to do with the military judiciary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At page 1, 2D 1262 -- thank you for that caution, document 2D 1262. Let me just state for the benefit of the Judges and the Prosecution, there was an error in the translation of this document, and you should have received the appropriate translation of this document separately. I hope you have it, but it is not in the binder. It was sent out separately. Mr. Buntic, on page 1 we can see that you attended the meeting, which was only logical, and I omitted to say that. On behalf of the Department for Defence, Mr. Bozo Rajic was present; in other words, Mr. Stojic was not there. Can we confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at page 17 of the Croatian version and page 19 of the English version. I'm told that it should state, in the transcript, that the document bears the following number: 2D 1262. That is fine. Under 19, the document lists the nominations for appointments. Pages 17 of the Croatian and 19 of the English versions contain the names of judges and prosecutors whom you appointed at this fifth meeting of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, can you tell Their Honours briefly in what way these proposals reached you, although this becomes quite evident while -- when one reads the discussions of the various attendees of this meeting? Tell us, what was the standard procedure? How did these proposals reach you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gathered proposals from municipalities and through the Party of Democratic Action and the Croatian Democratic Union. First we sought proposals from these two political parties which had won 90 per cent or more than 90 per cent of votes of the electorate. We were pressed for time. We had to gather information and approvals in order to be able to see these nominations through. As one can see from this document, we asked for the SDA to send in their proposals for judges and prosecutors of Bosniak ethnicity. Proposals were also sought from the municipal HDZ bodies for the judges of Croat ethnicity. Thereafter, discussions were held with Mr. Stojic or his deputy, Mr. Bozo Rajic, in order for us to be able to formulate proposals that would then be forwarded to the Presidency meetings. This was the customary procedure in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that since the Presidency did not meet regularly, following this particular Presidency meeting it was mostly the HVO that formulated these proposals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. After the 17th of October, 1992, the Presidency did not meet anymore, and the decisions on appointments of judges and prosecutors were made by the HVO of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I will skip several documents now. P00590, which is precisely the decree on district military prosecutors' offices in the territory of the HZ-HB, passed on the 17th of October, where under item 7 it reads that district military prosecutors and their deputies shall be appointed by the Presidency of the HZ-HB on proposals from the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is P00592. It's a decree on district military courts in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I'll just recall for the transcript that this is an exhibit, but P00587 is an exhibit under the same number. In para 20, it also says the judges and judge-jurors of the district military courts shall be appointed and relieved by the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the proposal of the chief of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is P00589, a decree establishing the section of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the territory of the HZ-HB. In Article 8, it says that it is the Presidency that makes appointments based on proposals by the chief of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, finally, the decree establishing the section of the Republican Public Prosecutor's Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In Article 4 it says that deputies to the public prosecutor shall be appointed by the Presidency of the HZ-HB, following proposals of the chief of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's document P00594. Mr. Buntic, to avoid going through all these documents in the binder individually, one by one, can we note that they confirm that the military -- that the Department of Justice mostly appointed judges, prosecutors and deputies? Can you just tell us, is that true of the last two decrees; namely, the appointment of judges to the section of the Supreme Court and appointments of deputies to the public prosecutor? Is it again the Department of Justice that approached the HVO with its proposals and nominations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious from these signatures that it is the Department of Defence that was responsible for appointments, and it is mainly the Department of Justice and General Administration that did that, which is why I gave the evidence I gave. So before this Court and under oath, I stated that if there had been any violations by judges, violations punishable under the Statute of this Tribunal, only the judges, themselves, can be held responsible for them, and I personally can be held, but certainly not the accused in this case. And I gave the reasons why any of these accused can be said to have made any violations; because they supported and contributed to the work of the courts to the best of their ability, and if there had been any interference and tampering with the work of the courts, then such interference did not come from any of the accused, but, if at all, from third parties who have been already convicted by valid judgements of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, could you just please look at the last document in this binder, named "Appointments." That's 1D 1612. Tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 1D 1612. That's just before the tab 3. You can see it on the screen. You have said that after 28th August, you were no longer head of the Justice Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Since I see that you attended this session of the 28th October 1993, and you made certain nominations for the positions of judges and prosecutors - that's page 4 in Croatian, page 3 in English, but for now it doesn't matter - you've already confirmed it's correct, can you just explain what, in your view, does it mean that from August, 28th of August, 1993, you were no longer the head of the Department of Justice, but you still attended sessions, nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a transition period from the day when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ceased to exist and the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna came into being. I believe that in the transition provisions, it was envisaged that the HVO continue to act as the government, pending the formation of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Since this was a package of laws concerning the judiciary, and especially the bill on the judicial council, of whom I later became the head, I attended this session, and I attended it also because I participated in the drafting of all these laws, together with Mr. Zubak, who at this time or perhaps a bit later became Minister of Justice, when the Cabinet was formed in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I understand you well, but do you believe that in this period from 28th August until the new government was elected, you had a kind of technical mandate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put it that way as well. That's a valid interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you mean that since you are appearing as a lawyer here and as a witness, and I cannot testify myself, do you think it is a position shared by other heads of departments who were not elected to the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all those who were heads of departments in the HVO, after the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ceased to exist, they continued to work with a technical mandate until the day when the government of the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna was elected. I believe that candidates -- nominees for ministers were known already in September 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I'd like to move on to the next subject that I hope we can deal with rather quickly; namely, reporting, reports from district military courts and district military prosecutors' offices. From the legislation we enumerated earlier governing this area, we saw that it was the responsibility of the Defence Department to submit these reports to the Presidency of the HZ-HB. Prior to your becoming head of the Justice Department, was it a practice or did you, as head of the Department of Justice, together with the Defence Department, did you make it a practice to submit aggregated reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from these reports and minutes and legislation, there were various situations. Reports on the work of courts was sometimes submitted to the Defence Department, sometimes to the Justice Department, in some cases to both. After that, aggregated reports were made and submitted to the HVO. In this document which appears first in section 3, there is an attempt to clarify this issue by instructing misdemeanor courts, military courts and military prosecutors' offices to submit their reports to the competent body, because what happened was that members of the Presidency who were heads of municipalities required the Justice Department to submit to them reports on the work of misdemeanor courts. We have already clarified this here. Misdemeanor courts were established by municipalities. They were financed by municipalities. Municipalities appointed judges -- that is, magistrates in misdemeanor courts, and it all worked on the level of municipalities. However, an absurd situation occurred where they wanted -- they, municipalities, wanted the Justice Department to submit to them reports on the work of courts which they, themselves, established and which were responsible to them and financed by them. So these were some of the absurd situations that we faced. We were responsible. We were appointed by the Presidency. We were answerable to the Presidency. They made the requests and demands they made, and this issue is clarified here. At least there is an attempt to clarify it. We gathered reports, and then, through the higher misdemeanor courts, we unified them in order to make some statistics. But there still occurred some absurd situations when we were asked to provide reports on the work of bodies that they formed, they financed, that answered to them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the record and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and everyone in the courtroom, you were commenting on the first document, that is, 1D 2004, just so we know what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can I just guide you with my questions -- in fact, not "may I," but I have to; it's my duty. And if I omit something, you will draw my attention. Have you ever seen, Mr. Buntic, the Defence Department, in the annual report to the government, or in any other report, did it ever summarise reports of the military courts and the military public prosecutors' offices and submitted them to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for the duration of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. The next document is a report that I'm not going to show to you, but for the Trial Chamber I wish to say that it's P04699. It is already an exhibit, and on page 47 you provide, among other things, the report on the establishment of district courts and prosecutors' offices. I'd like to ask you now: In your direct examination, you said that the judiciary actually started to work sometime in mid-1993. I'd like to ask you to look at the next two documents, P1842 and -- that's the first report from the District Military Prosecutors' Office in Mostar, and you said correctly from the 10th of April, 1993, it was made available to you and to the Defence Department. It's the report of the first trimester. Can we conclude that even in this shortened capacity, it operated, and in that period they received criminal reports, as we read in the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I need to correct you on one point. I did not say that the military judiciary bodies started working in the summer 1993. I believe I said a few days ago that district military courts started to operate and moved into their new premises sometime in the beginning of March, in the spring of 1993. That applies to military courts. Prosecutors' offices started to operate in end 1992, which is obvious from this document. But I fully appreciate the shortness of your time, and I would still like to point out one thing. This report partly answers the question asked a day or two ago by His Honour Judge Trechsel, when he asked me for information about the number of crimes against unknown -- that is, committed by unknown perpetrators, and the ratio of such crimes to the total. This report contains this information, and I am kindly asking you to read this report, because by reading it, we'll find out a lot about the work of the District Military Prosecutors' Office, if it can go against the time of the Trial Chamber, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If you believe that is important and if you believe it is important to the question of Judge Trechsel, you can do it against my time. We're talking about P1842; correct? Just tell us which page, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 1. It's the report on the work of the District Military Prosecutors' Office, Mostar, for the first three months of 1993, and it says that this prosecutor's office received a total of 114 criminal reports against 1.447 adults, 1 criminal report against four minors, and 6 criminal reports against perpetrators unknown. So we have a certain number of criminal reports against unidentified perpetrators. Out of the total criminal reports filed against adults, the military police of the HVO filed 92 criminal reports, the Department of Internal Affairs 18 criminal reports, the military police of the BH Army, the 4th Corps filed three criminal reports, whereas citizens filed one criminal report. In 20 cases, this prosecutor's office rejected the criminal report, in parentheses, which amounts to 17 per cent of the total number of reports filed, parenthesis closed, against 23 persons, in parentheses, 1.9 per cent of the total number of reports of persons against whom reports were made, parentheses closed. And I would only like to add this is a report of the then District Public Prosecutor, Mr. Mladen Jurisic, who currently occupies the highest judicial position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he's the president of the highest judicial council, and he has gone through vetting by the independent, International Judicial Commission and the services in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, thank you for the information. In this report -- but of particular interest are the criminal reports filed by the military police, and please look at that paragraph where it says that three such criminal reports were filed, and another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. If you allow me, let's stay with P1842. Look in your own language at the last paragraph on page 1. It seems that the military prosecutor indicated that out of the 1.302 individuals that were prosecuted, apparently there were 31 individuals that were prosecuted for crimes against humanity or crimes in international law. Are you aware of the fact that there were prosecutions for crimes against humanity, against obviously servicemen, because the military prosecutor is competent for military individuals? It would be interesting to know whether or how this number of 31 individuals is broken down and for what crimes against humanity. Was your attention drawn to this number of 31 individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already said the extent of what I know about it. This is a criminal report filed before the prosecutors' office for the case called Uborak, where some 80 dead bodies were recovered, and this was an act committed by the JNA. The 31 individuals listed in the criminal report went away with the Yugoslav Army. They were out of reach and the proceedings were at an impasse. One could not proceed prosecuting these individuals. To the best of my knowledge, this particular reference has to do with that case, where there was a large number of victims, and a criminal report was filed based on the charges of violations of international law. That's the extent of my knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are JNA numbers, but does this mean that the military prosecutor -- of course, if Mr. Jurisic was to come, we could ask him directly, but does that mean that the military prosecutor never charged for crimes against humanity in files regarding soldiers who may have committed crimes with a connotation of crimes against humanity or against international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As is quite evident from this document, there were such attempts on the part of the prosecutor to issue indictments for such crimes. However, Your Honour, I have to draw your attention to something I've mentioned before. The prosecutors' office became operational at the end of 1992 or in early 1993. Already in the month of May, there was an outbreak of the conflict between Muslims and Croats. The prosecutors' office were able to function smoothly for some five months and courts for some two to three months only. At that point, all these institutions were deprived of their facilities and case files were destroyed. And I'm referring to the month of May of 1993. We have a number of documents indicating the efforts that they made. However, in my view, the times did not allow them to do more. You know when this particular Tribunal was set up and when the first judgement was rendered. These were very complex crimes, entailing proceedings lasting up to three years in order for a proper judgement to be rendered. We have to bear in mind that this Tribunal had the United Nations' backing, a large budget, and the backing of this beautiful country, and it had this beautiful building at its disposal, and yet several years had to pass before the first judgement could be rendered for the crimes against humanity. We did not have the expertise that this particular Tribunal enjoys. We did not have the necessary documentation. We did not have the necessary exchanges of expertise. The persons who were involved in that did their best. You saw that the prosecutors' offices did issue indictments, and the courts did pass judgements. However, on charges for crimes against humanity, which are very complex cases, which carry a great burden of proof, in the cases where the perpetrators were out of reach, you know that even to this day Karadzic and Mladic remain out of reach of this Tribunal. What were the resources we had our disposal? Very few and far between. You will see, from this particular report, that there were cases of physical assault and harassment of judges by paramilitary formations of both the BH Army and the HVO. They worked under very difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to see a document. Ms. Nozica might speak to it later, 2D 506. I might be ahead of her, but this is to follow up on what you've just said. In July, the military prosecutor made another report on statistical activities. We know because we have in the indictment the issue of prisoners disappearing from the Vranica building in May. How is it that this case could not be registered or recorded in this July report of the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I'm able to see here, the first report relates to the first three months of work, that is to say, from the months of January through March, whereas the second report refers to the period through to the 9th of July, covering the first half of the year. I may have missed your reference. I'm not sure what you're referring to, but two different time periods are referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I note the time. I would like to finish this document and the related area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have another brief that reached you and your department, and that's something that you can confirm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 2D 506. I'm referring to the document Judge Antonetti drew your attention to, the one that you said referred to the first half of the year; that's to say, the 1st of January through to the 30th of June. Let's look at the criminal reports filed by the military police of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were four such criminal reports. Mr. Buntic, can you confirm that in this period of time, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina filed criminal reports to the District Prosecutors' Office in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite evident that these reports are referred to in both of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. The first one referred to three such criminal reports and the second one to four?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to see that criminal reports mostly arrived from the military police, some from the civilian MUP, and some from members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If the Army of the BH, in the report period, believed that crimes were committed against its members, it would only be logical for it to have filed or posit criminal reports to the Military Prosecutors' Office and they would consequently be covered by this report, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stop here and resume after the break. I still have several brief areas I want to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue, I'd like to say two things. First of all, by mistake, on page 27, line 7, we have "1992" instead of "1993," and I would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that according to my calculation, I've used up 95 minutes that you have allocated to me, but I would like your leave to finish my cross-examination, and the time that starts to run now you are to deduct from the time allocated to Mr. Stojic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, let us move to the subject of financing now, the financing of the military judiciary, and let me recall again that the basis -- the foundation for these questions now is your statement that the Defence Department was responsible, in terms of organisation, staff and finance, for the military judiciary. I would like you to tell us, to the best of your recollection, how district military courts and district military prosecutors' offices were financed at the time when you were head of the Justice Department, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military courts and military prosecutors' offices, if I remember well, were financed from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, from the funds allocated to the Defence Department. The uniforms, the logistics, the inventory, furnishings, equipment, and even buildings were provided by the Defence Department, by requisitioning, among other things, the law school building in Mostar, and the students were transferred to another location. That's how we had to make do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If you can remember, how were the salaries financed, when there was enough financing, for the judges and prosecutors in military courts and prosecutors' offices?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, through the Defence Department, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at document 1D 1180. It's the 41st session of HVO of the 9th of December, 1992. And if we can look at the last paragraph of these minutes, both in Croatian and in English. It says: "At the proposal of the Department of Justice and General Administration, the decision was made to allocate the amount of 5.000.000 Croatian dinars for the requirements of civilian, basic and higher courts and prosecutors' offices, as well as the amount of 1.476.000 for the requirements of the military court and the military prosecutors' office. Hereby your request from the HVO to allocate these funds for the military court and the military prosecutors' office." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have spoken about this already, and I believe these funds were needed for the renovation and adaptation of the building of the former Court and Associated Labour for the needs of the Municipal Court, that is, the civilian court. And in that building, in addition to the Municipal Court, there was also the higher prosecutors' office, civilian prosecutors' office, and the higher military prosecutors' office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a minute. You told me a moment ago that the Defence Department was in charge, in tactical terms, for the renovation of buildings and the supply of equipment, and now you're telling me that you are requesting funds from the HVO precisely for this technical aspect for military court and the military prosecutors' office? Just tell me "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I remember. In principle, the Department of Justice and General Administration did not finance either the military court or the military prosecutors' office, nor did these funds go through the Justice Department. I told you what I meant. You can see from here, 5.000.000 for civilian judiciary and just 1.476.000, and that could have been needed for the building of the court of the -- of Associated Labour which housed all these three bodies. And we are talking about end 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at 1D 2210. It's the next one in the binder. This is a document sent to the government of the HVO HZ-HB, the Justice Department, personally to Zoran Buntic. It is sent by the District Military Court in Travnik and the District Military Prosecutors' Office in Travnik. The signature below is the signature of the prosecutor and the president of the Court. It follows from this that they want you to pay out salaries for March, April, May, and June for the president of the Court, the judges and the administrative staff, as well as the prosecutor and his staff and administration. Do you remember this request, that it was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was sent, but I don't think these salaries came from the Department of Justice and General Administration. Yes, the request was sent, but I don't think the salaries went through the -- were paid out through our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It follows from this letter that they are owed salaries for March, April, May, and June. Do you know how they were financed before these months?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, have you had occasion to see the final account of the Defence Department for 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you seen a single document during your term of office from which it would follow that the Defence Department financed military judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but I also didn't see any documents stating that the Justice Department financed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To sum up this first segment, on the basis of what you said before this Court, namely, that the military and judiciary were, organisationally, in terms of staff and financially, linked to the Defence Department, is it the case on the basis of the documents I've shown you that you can confirm that in terms of staff, it was not exclusively relying on the Defence Department; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already have, several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents shown you, can you confirm that the Defence Department did not finance military courts and military prosecutors' offices, either, I'm saying on the basis of the documents I've shown you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the last series of questions relating to prisons, appointments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Ms. Nozica. I would like to put a question to the witness. It is possible that I misunderstood what he said, but maybe he can help me out. In response to a question posed by Ms. Nozica, who was asking you whether you could remember, on the basis of the documents available to you, if it was the Defence Department that financed the military courts, the district courts and the prosecutors' office, you answered, "No," and you couldn't remember, either, that this was done through the Justice Department. Therefore, could you tell us who was financing those courts as well as the prosecutors' office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have said that I believe the financing came from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg- Bosna, through the Defence Department. I said I believed that was so. I said -- I don't know if it's on the record -- that I hadn't seen a single document that could confirm what I've said. So, I wasn't saying that on the basis of documents, but rather on the basis of the regulations in force. On the basis of documents, I said I haven't seen a single document of that kind. I don't know how it was recorded, but that's what I said. So what I have said I said on the basis of the legislation that prevailed and on the basis of my belief that it was so, but I made a reservation, saying that I can't claim I have seen a document to that effect. That was the thrust of my answer. I don't know how it was conveyed to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much. That is what was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to move to a new subject now, the topic of military prisons. I want us to be very, very precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not going to examine you on centres for prisoners of war but on military prisons. Let us go back to a document you've seen before, 1D 2004, the first in that chapter. In item 15 of this document, that's page 4 in Croatian -- have you found it? You say the following: "During the war, the District Military Prison and the District Civilian Prisons in Busovaca, in Orasje, were established, and wardens were appointed for them. Also established was the District Prison in Mostar and the District Military Prison and the District Civilian Prison in Gabela. We emphasise that the supervision over the work and conditions in the District Prison is provided by the president of the Higher Court, whereas the supervision of the work and conditions in military prisons is provided by the Defence Department." That was the text, and now I will ask you several questions, one by one, about this paragraph, which is very important. You already said you were surprised there's no signature, but first of all, confirm what I've read.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you before that I wrote this document myself, and I stand by that answer. It's not signed, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, can you remember who established the District Military Prison and the District Civilian Prison in Orasje and who -- and at whose proposal appointed the wardens?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the question is irrelevant, Mr. President, as Orasje is beyond the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I wish to show something that may be important to the whole picture. If you acknowledge this observation, I would like to emphasise especially the second sentence, which says: "We emphasise that the supervision over the work and conditions in the District Prison is provided by the president of the Higher Court, whereas the supervision over the work and conditions in military prisons is provided by the Defence Department." As far as the district prisons in the indictment are concerned, if we want to know who supervised and controlled them, it is important to show the entire picture. If you allow me, I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you remember, Witness, who established the District Military Prison and the District Civilian Prison in Orasje and who appointed the wardens?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember well, we received a proposal from Bosanska Posavina for the district military and district civilian prisons in Orasje, and the HVO passed a decision to establish the district military and district civilian prisons in Orasje. I believe there was a proposal for the appointment of the wardens which came from Bosanska Posavina, that is, Orasje, and the decision was made along those lines by the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll skip the District Prison in Busovaca. How about the one in Mostar that was a civilian prison? It is not important to our story.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no decision needed to be made because it existed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The District Military Prison and the District Civilian Prison in Gabela, do you remember who established them and who passed the decision to establish this prison and appoint the wardens?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered this question. I do not remember that the HVO made such a decision, and I do not remember that it was promulgated in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. As for what you said, which is important, namely, the supervision over the district civilian and military prisons, I would like us to follow the sequence and look at the next document, which is P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica, but I would like to ask the witness a question about this document, and I hope I'm not repeating a question someone else has put before. I would like to know how come that you, the Minister of Justice and Administration, file a report on the Military Prosecutors' Office and district military courts. I had assumed that you had said that they were separated; the military jurisdiction is under the Minister of Defence and the civilian jurisdiction is under the Ministry of Justice and General Administration. Then I failed to understand why you would even bother to file a report with such a title and contents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the issue is clarified in the first items of this report or, namely, in item 1. The events took their own course, as item 1 clearly states. I observe that the -- that a report on the work of the department is sought which normally does not submit reports. However, acknowledging the intention and the wish to introduce as much order in the state of affairs, and honouring the conclusions from the working meeting, what is meant here is the meeting of the HVO, the department submits a report on the judiciary for the aforementioned period. It is quite evident from this that the HVO of the HZ-HB ordered the Justice Department to produce a report on the work of all the courts and prosecutors' offices, regardless of their civilian or military nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I take cognizance of your explanations. I'm still a bit puzzled, because in other situations when the question was how the situation in prisons were, you were very strict in respecting the limits of your competencies, as you told us, and I fail -- I frankly fail to see how you improve order by reporting on something which is not within your competencies. But, I mean, you have given an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. I've explained why, but it was precisely for this reason that I made this statement, and I stand by it fully. If there was something unlawful or incriminating in the work of courts and prosecutors' offices, for precisely those reasons I assume upon myself all the responsibility and I invite the Prosecutor before this Tribunal to issue an indictment against me where there are grounds for it, because where it comes to the work of the courts, I can be the sole responsible individual for the period we're discussing up until the 28th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to be sure I understand you correctly, you say you take all responsibility also for the military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the work of both military and civilian courts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to go back to the question you put. Mr. Buntic quoted the first sentence, where he says: "We note that a report is sought from a department to which such reports are not submitted." We looked a moment ago at a report, which is document P1842, and another document, 2D 00506. These were reports on the work of the District Military Prosecutors' Office in Mostar for the first three months and for the first half of the year. As we can see, the reports were submitted both to you and to the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already done that, I've already confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going back to that issue, because there might be some confusion about the party to whom the reports were delivered to, and that's the document 1D 2004. Let's look at another document, P3350. This is another report which you signed, which you made on the work of the Justice Department, and that's from the 1st of January, 1993, until the 31st of June. Let us look at item 11, where you confirm precisely what you've mentioned now; the establishment of the district prisons. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, 1D 1184. That's the next document in the binder. These are minutes from the 35th meeting of the HVO, held on the 9th of April, 1993; page 5 of the Croatian version and the last paragraph of the last page of the English version, which says: "At the proposal of the Department of Justice and General Administration of the HVO HZ-HB, as warden of the Military and Civilian District Prison in Orasje, Ilija Benkovic is appointed, and for the warden of the District Prison in Mostar, Pero Nikolic." Can you confirm that this is precisely the situation that you recalled, and that is that in Orasje, the proposal went through the Justice Department to Orasje and that's how the appointment was made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described precisely what happened. The proposal arrived from Posavina, from Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, thank you. We have all of that in the transcript. Let me just say that this document confirms the situation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not confirming your question. It does not confirm your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me what is wrong in the question I put to you and what the actual state of affairs was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is erroneous is that the proposal came from the Justice Department or that I sent the proposal. I said who the proposal came from and answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, there is no need to be incensed about it. I merely read out what the minutes said.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes are erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at the following document, 1D 1105. This is a document approving the appointment of the prison staff for convicts of misdemeanor and criminal offences, dated the 2nd of March, 1993, signed by the president of the Croatian Defence Council, Pero Markovic.
