You were shown the document during the examination-in-chief, and you said that this referred to the serving of sentences for misdemeanor offences and that it went -- and that it fell within the jurisdiction of the municipal HVO organs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In accordance with the law on the serving of criminal and misdemeanor sentences, municipalities can set up prisons for the serving of such sentences, and this was the case in Capljina, where the municipality set up a prison for precisely such sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I went back to this document for a very important word which is contained in the heading, which says: "... granting permission to the misdemeanors prison and the detention facility." Can you confirm that detention falls within criminal sanctions, or can you confirm for us that it was only a judge of either a regular civilian or military court could order detention?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a misdemeanors magistrate would not be able to order detention. He could do so in a summary procedure, ordering detention as an urgent measure, but I don't believe that a summary procedure would include detention. It would include the immediate rendering of the judgement and the holding in custody of the person convicted. I don't believe that the misdemeanors court could do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can it follow from this particular document that what was referred to was only a detention facility and not a place where misdemeanor sanctions were served?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could interpret it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I haven't objected yet, I don't believe, to the many leading questions that have been put to the witness during the course of this examination, whether we call it a direct or a cross, but this is in fact a direct examination, in that it is intended to lead evidence that's favourable. It's not undermining the witness's credibility or to attempt to deal with alleged incriminating issues that were led by counsel for Mr. Prlic on the direct. So just so we're clear again, and I've said it previously last week in respect of the examination that was conducted by counsel for Mr. Coric, and I just want to put that out there again for the Trial Chamber, we've gone very far afield from what was led in the direct examination. Sure, the direct examination touched on detention facilities, but we have now and consistently been at a level of detail that is such that it can only really barely be classified as direct examination. Counsel's putting on her case. She's using her time to do it, and she's certainly doing her job in that respect, but let's just be fair about what's happening here. These are documents provided to the Prosecution the other day, on Thursday. We're well beyond, really, the scope of the direct, and I think that in this situation, leading questions are extremely unfair. And at the very least, I want to point out that the leading questions and the answers that they generate should very definitely be given a reduced probative value by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you say, Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me respond by saying that this is pure cross-examination. The document was shown to the witness, and the witness answered the question to the best of his abilities. When it comes to leading questions, I am within cross-examination and completely in keeping with the Rules. Let me stress that I am now using up the time allocated to the Defence of Mr. Stojic, and I was merely putting questions to the witness on the subjects raised in the examination-in-chief. There was one subject that went beyond that scope, and as you can see, most of the documents are marked "1D," therefore documents that were used in the examination-in-chief. It is very important to me, and it was rightly put by the Prosecutor, that I find answers to these questions very important, and I would not like to have any technical impediment, such as putting of improper questions to the witness, to get in the way of my examination, so please caution me about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you're telling us that since the documents were tackled during the direct examination, you are in cross-examination, this is no new topic; however, you do agree to that time being taken out of your overall time because you went over the time that was allocated? Have I summarised your position well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are absolutely right. This is cross-examination, but regardless of the fact that this is cross-examination, it is deducted from the time allocated to Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, if you look at the detail I've drawn your attention to, can you tell us whether this involves the employment of staff for a prison where individuals serve misdemeanor sentences or is it also a facility where individuals are remanded into custody by order of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this particular decision was in keeping with the municipal regulations. However, this is also a detention and a facility in Capljina, so the HVO went beyond the scope of their powers. As I've already said, they overstepped the powers granted by the law to the Capljina local authorities. But the decision is as it is. It says "for the serving of misdemeanor sentences," and the Capljina barracks are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the first name on the list there, Bosko Previsic? Do you know whether he was perhaps hired in some other prison in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that indeed he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You can't remember where that was, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at another document concerning the control over the prisons. We are talking about the establishment and supervisional control over military prisons, and we are referring back to the report of yours, where you said that the supervision of work and state of affairs in prisons is done by the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what it reads, then it's a mistake. It should fall within the purview of the president of the District Military Court. If this is indeed what is written there, then it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to prisons. Now, when it comes to the venues holding prisoners of war, that's where the Defence Department would have jurisdiction. Now, where it comes to -- when it comes to prisons, it's the president of the District Court and the warden of the prison who have those responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then it must have been a slip or an error on your part in drafting the report. Let us look at the next document, 1D 1797. This is a report from the District Military Court in Mostar, submitted to the Defence ministry, government, administration of the military police and the crime department. Let's look at the first sentence. What does the president of the District Military Court say? On the 6th of November, 1993, the president of the Mostar District Military Court, pursuant to Article 205 of the ZKP, performed an inspection of detainees at the VIZ in Ljubuski. Mr. Buntic, we've seen this document before. Can you confirm that this is precisely the situation where you said that the supervision of the military court lay within the hands of the president of the court with territorial jurisdiction and the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms my statement that I made immediately before looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at another document, 2D 1412. This is a document sent to the Justice Department, to the Department of Justice and Administration, and to the commander of the OZ Central Bosnia, Colonel Blaskic, sent by the District Prison Kaonik-Busovaca, signed by the warden of the prison. In this letter, the warden of the prison, and undoubtedly it's the district military prison, says that for safety and legality of the functioning, the person responsible is the warden, which is only logical.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Item 2 says treatment of imprisoned individuals in the section for custody before trial of the District Military Prison is under the responsibility of the warden of the District Military Prison and under the supervision of the president of the District Military Court in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under the administration of the director and under the supervision of the Department for Justice and General Administration of the HZ-HB. So in the third category, we have convicts. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The District Military Prison could no way have been under the jurisdiction of the Justice and General Administration Department. This is a proposal of Zlatko Aleksovski. He is just proposing something. It is not an official decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, according to the legislation that prevailed, and I mean primarily the decree on district military courts, who was in charge and under what legislation were sentences served? We are now moving into subjects that I haven't prepared for, but I'm asking you: Military men who were convicted by competent military courts, under whose jurisdiction did they serve sentences?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This matter is governed by Article 30 through Article 35 of the Decree on District Military Courts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of the 17th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please answer me. Do you know under whose jurisdiction were convicts? Who was responsible for them when they were serving their sentences? We have the decree. Just answer my question. Nothing is problematic with the document. It's already an exhibit. We can all analyse it. Who had jurisdiction, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Persons who were legally convicted and who were convicted by district military courts and who are serving sentences.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that they were under the supervision of the president of the District Military Court and the warden or the administrator of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. Now, in conclusion, I will avail myself of your presence in the courtroom, Mr. Buntic, to establish certain provisions in the Law on Criminal Procedure, an issue that was raised during your direct examination, and I hope you can be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in explaining how it was stipulated in the period we are discussing. You have a large document in front of you. It's not in the binder. It's a separate document. I think it was given to you. Could the usher please assist Mr. Buntic, if necessary. I'm speaking of the document 4D 01105, and that's the Law on Criminal Procedure. Mr. Buntic, can you confirm that it was precisely this law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was taken over from -- that was taken over by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and applied in this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Penal Code not of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslav that was taken over, as such, by virtue of the republic decree and further taken over by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and applied in the territory of the HZ-HB. So it was originally a federal law on criminal procedure of the SFRY that was applied in the territory of HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You explained very nicely these steps. So after the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was internationally recognised, this law was taken over, and then it was further taken over by the HZ-HB, and it was applied by the HZ-HB in full; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we were talking about continued prosecution, I want to emphasise certain points. Please look at Article 60 [as interpreted]. Can you look at Article 6 very quickly. I know you can do it, as a lawyer. It governs precisely the area you talked about. In every case when the public prosecutor finds there are no grounds for prosecution, the prosecutor informs the injured party that they can continue prosecution themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, a situation is described when the public prosecutor renounces the indictment, and in that case the injured party may adhere to the indictment or issue a new indictment. You've mentioned that, too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Paragraphs 4, 5 and 6 further elaborate the rights of the injured party when he finds that the public prosecutor gave up on the case or when he died, so it protects basically all the rights of the injured party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They enable the injured party to continue with the prosecution, regardless of the prosecutor's decision to abandon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are also familiar with the current legislation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Law on Criminal Procedure; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you at least answer this question, if you know: Does the injured party still have these same rights when the new law has been adopted by the highest standards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the new Penal Code in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the rights of the injured party are considerably reduced, compared to the arrangements in the Law on Criminal Procedure that we are looking at and that was applied in HZ-HB, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasegovic-Tomic showed you one document that I'm not going back to, but I'm just going to just remind you it was the decision whereby the prosecutor abandons the prosecution. It's page -- it's 5D 4175, the first page, and the prosecutor there invokes Article 180 [as interpreted]. Can you look at Article 180 [as interpreted]? The legal recourse. It says the investigating judge shall terminate the investigation when the public prosecutor informs him that he abandoned the prosecution. And it says that the investigating judge shall inform the injured party of dismissal of the investigation within eight days. Was it really like that in practice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and I believe that's the arrangement that was cited by the Coric Defence, yes, relative to the document 5D 04175.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's Article 170, not 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have been told that on page 56, line 16, the article mentioned should be "170" instead of "180." Let us now look at Article 181 of this law that deals with the questions asked by the Trial Chamber; namely, what can the injured party do if no action is taken on the criminal report in which he or she is the injured party? This article says: "The parties and the injured parties may always file a complaint with the president of the court before which proceedings are being conducted because of procrastination or other irregularities in the course of the investigation. The president of the court shall investigate the allegations in the complaint, and if the proponent has so requested, shall inform him of what action has been taken." This seems to confirm what you have said, Mr. Buntic; namely, the parties, too, the prosecution and the defence and even the injured parties themselves, have the right to address the president of the court whenever they believe that their rights are infringed upon due to undue delays?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I said that complaints were possible against the work of the prosecutor, even, and such complaints were to be addressed to the higher prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just want to confirm with these provisions which you said; namely, that they are grounded in this law. Let us now look at Article 205. It's a provision governing the issue of supervision over courts -- over prisons, sorry, and inmates. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says: "Supervision over prisoners in custody shall be exercised by the president of the court who is authorised to do so." Para 2 stipulates in which way this is to be done, and para 3 states that the president of the court shall do so possibly in cooperation with the public prosecutor. That's what you said when we were talking about supervision over military prisons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this confirms all the evidence I've given on this subject; namely, that presidents of courts, if we are talking about military courts, provide supervision, and when civilian prisons are concerned, it is the presidents of civilian courts. If I had made a slip of the tongue, it was just a slip of the tongue. These things happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Of course, of course. That is why I am here to establish what is correct and what is not, and we have all these documents in evidence. And the last article I want to deal with is 346. One of the Judges asked you about the legal qualification of the Act cited in the criminal report or the decision to carry out an investigation, to issue an indictment and judgement. Article 346 states that the judgement may only refer to the person who is indicted, which is logical, and only to the act cited in the indictment and in the trial, and para 2 says the Court shall not be bound by the recommendations of the Prosecutor concerning the legal qualification of the Act. Mr. Buntic, it is unequivocal that the Court was authorised to qualify the act the way they saw fit, based on the description given in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to be made on the basis of the description in the indictment which was prepared by the Prosecution, but it was the Court that decided on the legal qualification.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about the filing of criminal reports for war crimes. I know that criminal law is not your primary field of expertise, but you do have certain knowledge. Do you remember that under the Penal Code prevailing at the time, war crimes encompassed rapes and thefts and forced removal for performing forced labour; all these were elements of the crime of war crime, in fact, during the state of war in the conditions specified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were stipulated by the law as crimes. To the extent I remember the Penal Code of the SFRY and the Penal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did not qualify these acts as war crimes. The police filed criminal reports about what they observed, and they were not required to compile that report including qualification. The police had to file a criminal report based on what they knew, saying that a crime had occurred. A criminal report never had to be a formal document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm trying to say. If the criminal report, itself, did not contain a legal qualification, and even the indictment sometimes didn't, the Court was certainly not bound to follow that legal qualification. I have no further questions. I thank the Trial Chamber for the additional time given me. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica. I believe my fellow Judge wants to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours, but it is my turn before Madam Alaburic. I announced a short cross-examination of some 10 to 15 minutes and a couple of questions. The cross-examination will have to do with what Mr. Buntic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Judge Mindua has a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Counsel, I had asked for the floor before you started. Witness, I have a question for you. Indeed, when I read page 47 of the transcript, at line 9, I was a little nonplussed with regard to the minutes that were written during meetings, during HVO meetings. Let me be more specific. Regarding -- I'm looking for the document number. One moment, please -- 1D 1184, we looked at it a few minutes ago. This is a proposal for appointment of a warden, including the Mostar Prison warden, and you opposed Ms. Nozica's question. You said that these minutes were erroneous. Therefore, I'm asking you how the minutes were taken. They were HVO meetings, and more specifically the meeting of the 35th session. Was it recorded, which were the means available to the participants, including you, because you mentioned as one of them which were the means at your disposal, in order to check the minutes? For instance, at the following meeting, did you have the minutes available to approve them, oppose them, or possibly amend them? Do you understand my question, because you said that the document was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm quite certain that in the course of my examination, we presented, as evidence, this proposal which came from Orasje. I can't recall the number of the document, but I'm sure that it was adduced as evidence during my testimony. This was not my proposal or a proposal I sent. The proposal came from Orasje and was placed, as such, as an item on the agenda. As is well known, the district civilian and district military prisons were established as one in Orasje, although -- one, although with separate departments. The document which came from Orasje and which included a nomination for the warden of the prison became an item of the agenda and was adopted by the HVO. I said that the error consisted in the fact that it was not my proposal. The proposal arrived as it was in writing from Orasje, after it had been formulated in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And since then, have you not had an opportunity to read the minutes and possibly to ask for them to be amended, because we know you were the head of that department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had that opportunity, and I most likely missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, in your answer, and I wish to test the interpretation and the record, you said something that struck me. You said you spoke of -- "I am quite certain that in the course of my examination, we presented as evidence this proposal." This sounds very much like an identification with the Defence. Did you say that and did you mean it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I had the document before me in the days of my testimony which had been sent from Orasje, containing nominations for the warden - that was Ilija Benkovic. The minutes have accurate information, but as I have said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. No doubt I have badly expressed myself, because you are not answering at all the question that I put. I am speaking of your words on line 5 of page 61, where you spoke of your examination and then said: "... we presented as evidence this proposal." "We presented," who do you mean, "we presented as evidence"; the evidence here that you were presenting together with the Defence or something else? I just want clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the entire Tribunal. I'm sorry if I made a mistake. I meant this particular Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Trechsel, my colleague tells me that she heard that the gentleman indicated that it was presented, not "we presented," and again -- so -- and certainly, I mean, if you want to pose the question whether he's our -- identifies with Dr. Prlic, go ahead. I mean, they're not closely related. But, I mean, I think what he said was "it was presented."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you very directly answered my question, and this is exactly what I wanted to provoke a possibility to clarify any error in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm listening to you in English, and I can understand your English, and I think your English is being translated into B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's possible. Of course, it's a constant danger, as we all know who work with translations, and I'm sure it will be verified and rectified. But this was the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think it was a good question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to the Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. My cross-examination will have to do with a part of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Buntic recorded on pages 30245, lines 2 to 6. That's the transcript of the 7th of July. That's a portion from the very start of Mr. Buntic's testimony, speaking of his engagement in the military HVO, in the Crisis Staff as it was at the time, and its participation in the liberation of Mostar and parts of the municipalities of Capljina and Mostar in 1992, between the months of April and June of 1992. These are the issues on which I will put questions to Mr. Buntic, since this is cross-examination, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In your evidence, you said that you were the deputy commander of the battalion. Can you tell us who was the commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the late Pero Pehar was the commander of the battalion, of the Citluk Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was the Citluk Battalion -- my apologies, Your Honour. Yes, I will be mindful. We have everything on the record. Fine. Did the Citluk Battalion have subunits or were these individuals originally from the area of Citluk, from that municipality, and what was its title?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title was "Brotnjo Battalion." It had six companies from the territory of the Municipality of Citluk, an anti-sabotage detachment, sabotage detachment, an anti-aircraft platoon, a signals platoon, technical platoon. At any rate, all of its members hailed from the area of Citluk Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of the company commanders, at least some of them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I can. The commander of the 1st Company was Mr. Blago Pehar. The commander of the 2nd was Tonco Juric. The commander of the 3rd was Mladen Sevo. The commander of the 4th was Coric. I can't remember the first name at the moment. The commander of the 5th was, I believe, Mr. Planinic. And the commander of the 6th was, I believe, Zjelko Ostojic. That was the Medjugorje-Bijakovici Company. The commander of the Anti-Aircraft Company was Zdenko Bozic. The commander of the Anti-Sabotage Detachment was Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see your memory serves you well. Did the Brotnjo Battalion take part in the actions aimed at liberating Mostar or, rather, the surgeon areas of Capljina, Stolac, in the area of the Dubrovnik Plateau, in the area of 1992, let me add?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It participated in an action called "Lipanjska Zora," which was launched in the night between the 6th and the 7th of June, by engaging two of its companies, the Anti-Sabotage Detachment and one volunteer company which had been specially prepared for that action and was composed of volunteers from all companies. The strength was of some 200 to 240 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in that action?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know if Zjelko Ostojic participated in the action?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zjelko Ostojic, the commander of the Bijakovici-Medjugorje Company also took part in the action.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us go back from the month of June to the month of April of 1992. We had occasion here to hear a witness in a document 3D 00595, which is already in evidence. For the sake of time, let me just ask you this: Do you have any knowledge about the refugees from the Dubrovnik Plateau, from the town of Stolac and the municipality of Stolac, Pocitelj, back in 1992, the month of April; and if so, can you tell us what it is that you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in the month of April and early May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, 1992. I'm afraid that the fatigue is getting the better of me. I believe that Their Honours know what the strategic importance of the Dubrovnik Plateau was, which covered parts of the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina and Mostar, and the eastern bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Is that the Dubrovnik Plateau or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dubrovski -- Dubrava Plateau, sorry, yes. It comes from the name of "Dubrava."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I see "Dubrovnik" was entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was probably said already, between the 18th and the 19th of September, the JNA deployed a large contingent of its forces there and captured the plateau. In the subsequent month or so, it chased away all the Croats from the area and continued its breakthrough toward Dubrovnik or, rather, towards Slano with one wing of its forces, and the other wing of its forces went towards Mostar and the Heliodrom airport, where they landed. In the following couple of days, they captured the entire municipality of Mostar and deployed their forces on the boundaries of the municipality of Mostar. And I believe that Their Honours are aware of the fact that the Mostar municipality borders with the Citluk municipality. In the months of April and May of 1992, the JNA forced out of the area all of the Bosniaks, too. Thus, the situation was such that on the left bank of the Neretva River, there were tens of thousands of Bosniaks that had been driven away from the area by the JNA. This called for an urgent intervention on our part. A meeting was held of the Command Staff for the Eastern Zone. Mr. Praljak was headquartered in Citluk at the time. Urgent orders were issued for a makeshift bridge to be constructed across the Neretva in order for us to take in the Bosniaks. All of that was organised in the course of the night, and we started receiving these tens of thousands of persons who were driven out. On that bank -- rather, that bank of the River Neretva was under the control of my 6th Company, the Bijakovici-Medjugorje Company, the commander of which was Zjelko Ostojic. The order was issued for the population to be received and for accommodation to be found for them. As a result, the civilian protection was issued with the orders to put these people up somewhere. I know that subsequently, this was organised in the following way: Those individuals who wanted to join our ranks and join our struggle to take control over the Dubrava Plateau again were given that opportunity. Others were put up in the elite hotel resort of Kompas which could receive 400 individuals. Two more private homes were set aside for that same purpose, and some 400 to 500 Bosniak Muslims declared themselves willing to stay there and join our fight to wrest the Dubrava plateau from the JNA control. Those who wished to stay there -- or, rather, those who wished to leave, including women, children and the elderly, were given that possibility. In the night between the 6th and the 7th of June, we set out in the -- set out and launched the action of -- that I've mentioned before, Lipanjska Zora. My company was in such a state that I believed I ought to march ahead of them. It is true that on the 7th of June, we liberated a section of the eastern bank of the Neretva, the area of Sevac Njive, where we had previously had great losses in our companies. The first one to my right got killed and three of them to my left were seriously wounded. Now, why did I survive is something I find difficult to explain today, but this is the way things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Those civilians, those over 10.000 civilians that were transferred, were they Croats, or were they Croat Bosniaks, or were they all civilians who were unable to stay?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe over 90 per cent were Bosniak Muslims, because Croats had been expelled from that area before that. And out of those whom we put up in this resort, Kompas Medjugorje, I know that we've given them uniforms and weapons, and we even trained them militarily. All this was done so that we could recover the Dubrava Plateau together. I believe that those 300, 400 people who were put up in Kompas Medjugorje Resort later formed the Bregova [phoen] Brigade, composed primarily of the Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Buntic. My cross-examination is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think the best would be to have the break now. I would like to inform Mr. Karnavas that in the afternoon, the Witness and Victims Unit informed us that Witness Zuzul will arrive on Monday evening, which means that he can be cross-examined on Tuesday. We will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Witness Zuzul will arrive on Sunday evening, not on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I would like to make a correction to the transcript. I said that Witness Zuzul would arrive on Sunday, and not on Monday; line 23, page 68. Witness Zuzul will arrive on Sunday and not on Monday. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Judges. Good afternoon, my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Before I announce the subject of my cross-examination, Mr. Buntic, I would like us to tell the Trial Chamber if we have seen each other before ever, if we have ever discussed the case at all.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we have never seen each other before. We have never discussed anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, briefly about the topics of my cross-examination, which I believe are completely linked to direct examination. First of all, we'll have some clarifications --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask for all extra microphones in the courtroom to be switched off. We cannot hear Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- then we have to deal with the actions of the government, that is, the civilian authorities, with regard to the defence of Bosnia. The third subject will be -- my colleagues tell me that the first topic I mentioned is not recorded, so I will start from the beginning, announcing the subjects of my cross-examination, which I believe are completely reliant upon direct examination. First we will make some clarifications with regard to the actions of the civilian HVO, that is, the government. Then I will try to discuss with the witness the activities of the civilian HVO, that is, the government, in affairs related to the defence of Herceg-Bosna. This will be followed by a brief clarification of topics related to the Law on Criminal Procedure and Criminal Prosecution, and this will be followed by a brief clarification about military units that were in the territory of Citluk and adjacent municipality in the summer of 1992. After that, if any time is left and if I conclude that it is still necessary after the answers Mr. Buntic gives me, I will ask a few questions about exchanges of prisoners and detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Buntic, a few clarifications about the actions of the civilian HVO, that is, the government. You have already explained that from the day the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established on the 28th of August, 1993, the HVO continued to operate as the government. And then you explained the role of the HVO as a ministry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot quite confirm this, in this language. In the transitional period between HZ-HB and the establishment of the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO continued in a technical mandate. But from the day the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna appointed its own government, the ministers, too, were appointed. I cannot say with the same powers, because the powers were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I want to read to you from the document that we have discussed in direct examination. It is not prepared in my set of documents. It's the decision to establish the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It's document 1D 1677. Article 12 of this document states that the functions of state authorities, including appointments, shall be vested in the bodies of government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From that day onwards, we have seen numerous documents, and we will see many more, which the civilian HVO again signs as the government, and certain sections of the HVO sign as ministries. That is indeed how the bodies signed in that transitional period starting in August, in end August?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In August 1993, did there occur any change in the scope of work of the government, that is, ministries, compared to the period prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that under this transitional provision, pending the appointment of the Government of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO continued to discharge functions that had been prescribed by the statutory decision of the HZ-HB, with the same powers and with those limitations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In November 1993, the government is formed under the decision to establish the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, with the proviso, as I've said before, that the names of the future ministers, the ministers to be, were already known in September 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Buntic, in November 1993 or perhaps earlier, did there occur any changes in the legislation governing the scope of work of the government and individual ministries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I remember. The regulations of the HZ-HB continued to be observed until new regulations of the Croatian Republic were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I want to explain to the Trial Chamber certain details about the promulgation of legislation in the Official Gazette. In the former Yugoslavia, was it a duty of every municipality and association of municipalities and republics and provinces to promulgate their legislation in some official gazette?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I've said this already. From the basic administrative unit, municipality, autonomous province, republic, and up to the federal state, everyone was duty-bound to make public, in official gazettes, the legislation they passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the record. Can I just say the last part of the sentence "from the municipality to the federal level" is not recorded. And let me use this opportunity to correct page 72, line 3. The year is 1993, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Buntic, relative to this duty to promulgate legislation, was it the same for enterprises and other entities, even if they published their rules on a board?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All companies or legal persons, until 1989, all of them were socially owned. They were duty-bound to publish their general documents, their statutes, their rules of procedure, their self-management agreements and social compacts, and they did so on advertising boards or their internal gazettes. Organisations usually had their own internal gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, now in view of all that we have already said, could we agree also with the conclusion that the fact that one territorial community publishes its regulations in an official gazette is no proof that that territorial unit is a state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. We have already seen that even municipalities had their own official gazettes, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is an association of municipalities. And the public nature and transparency of work required that all regulations and new rules be published in an official gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell the Trial Chamber whether municipality in the former Yugoslavia were organised in such a way as to have an assembly, which was a kind of legislative body, they had executive councils as executive bodies, and within their purview they had the right to appoint judges of local courts or misdemeanor courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The organisation of municipal authority was structured in such a way that municipalities had their Assembly as the highest body of administration, the body that passed laws that were within the purview of the municipality. They had their own executive councils, which practically enforced the legislation passed by the Assembly. Municipalities selected and appointed judges for misdemeanor courts and municipal civilian courts, that is, first-instance courts. They had the right to elect and relieve judges, and they had the duty to finance municipal courts, regardless of whether they were misdemeanor courts or regular first-instance courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This division into the legislative, executive and judicial authority, was it -- did it apply to other levels of authority; autonomous provinces, republics, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the internal structure of bodies of government was copied from the highest level, the federal state, to the lowest level, the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of what has been said, could we agree with the following conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: After hearing your answer, I would like to ask a question. But, please, I did not want to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Ms. Alaburic should state what her conclusion is first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interruption now has happened, and I have a very, very elementary question. We hear the word "misdemeanor" repeated again and again. Could you tell the Chamber, what is the definition of a misdemeanor as opposed to, what, a crime, or a felony, or a contravention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the law on minor offences or misdemeanors, misdemeanors were acts of lesser or insignificant danger to the society or acts which resulted in minor consequences. Usually, in practice, traffic violations that did not cause any grave consequence, such as great material damage, fatality or serious bodily injury were treated as a misdemeanor. A serious car accident would be a crime if it resulted in a fatality, in serious material damage and serious bodily injury. All the rest were misdemeanors. That included speeding, which was the most frequent form of traffic violation; that is, in the field of traffic. Also, all the legislation in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, stipulated which acts were misdemeanors in a certain category, and the sentences that could be meted out. Sixty days imprisonment was the maximum sentence for a misdemeanor, and there were also fines envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's a very precise answer, and I now know where we are. Thank you very much. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will return to our territorial units now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After what we've said, my proposed conclusion that I want you to agree with or not is this: The fact that one territorial unit has a kind of legislative, a kind of executive and a kind of judicial authority, is no proof that that territorial unit is a state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, because these are not the constitutive elements of a state. I don't think this Court needs an explanation on what the elements of a state are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No need to explain. Over the past few days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I do have a question. Thanks to Ms. Alaburic, I have become cognizant of something very interesting. Through her questions, she elicited from you that judges of basic courts were elected by their municipalities. I did not know that. This is something new to me. In the federal system, that's how things worked. Automatically, judges of basic courts were elected by the municipalities. This is the federal system; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the way it was in every municipality in the former Yugoslavia, with a proviso that there was a possibility that several municipalities had a common basic court. Such was the example of the Basic Court in Mostar. The Basic Court in Mostar was established for three municipalities; the Mostar municipality, Nevesinje municipality and Citluk municipality. In that Basic Court in Mostar, judges were elected in agreement with all three municipalities and financed by all three municipalities proportionately to their respective populations. That's how it worked in principle. There existed some exceptions. That's why it was called "Basic Court" and not a municipal court, because there was a possibility that several municipalities share the same basic court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, over the past days, on several occasions you said that defence had been a priority on several occasions, so that both the civilian and military police forces were engaged in combat activities because the priority was to defend the territory of Herceg-Bosna from attacks by either armies. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I, as the commander of the defence for Citluk, used the reserve force of the civilian police in order to cover several sections of the frontline which were not fully covered because of exhaustion. We even had certain cases where we were attacked by toxic warheads. For that reason, the civilian police had to sometimes be engaged along the frontline, and this was true even more so for the military police, which was engaged even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the civilian HVO, in other words, the government, take care of the interests of the defence of Herceg-Bosna in its work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war and for as long as there was an immediate threat of war, the most immediate objective was to defend the territory or part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When my friend Karnavas showed you document P00559, which is the minutes from the 6th meeting of the HVO, held on the 7th of October, 1992, where, among other things, the organisation of courts was discussed, too. At that time, there were two versions which were put forth as a proposal, and His Honour Judge Trechsel had a question to put to that. There was an explanation provided along with the second version or variant which proposed the setting up of a system which would be outside of the judiciary system of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The explanation was, I quote: "What is at risk is the complete collapse of the defence exercise because of the non-functioning of the courts." My question to you is: Did the HVO or the government, while organising the judiciary, take into account the interests of the defence of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents I had before me, which were tendered by the Stojic Defence, included, I believe, minutes wherein a discontentment of the head of the Defence Department was expressed because judges had not been previously elected for military courts. I believe that that criticism was quite justified. The two versions or variants we referred to earlier, I believe I explained extensively. Version number 2 was proposed earlier on. However, after the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement in Medjugorje, dated the 21st of July, we, and I mean the deputy -- or, rather, the justice minister and I agreed and issued a decree on district military courts, district military prosecutors' offices, departments of the Supreme Court, and Republican prosecutors' office, because those had been harmonised with the relevant legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was the establishment of the Military Prosecutors' Office also in the service of the defence of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Something that happens in all times of war is desertion, abandonment of posts, impossibility to mobilise fresh forces, and whatever normally happens in other parts of the world also happened in that region, and it had to be regulated in some way. We said that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already placed out of force the federal law on military courts and military prosecutors' offices, and that particular area had to be regulated in some way. We discussed various versions or variants, but I believe it is quite clear which of these we opted for ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One of the topics you referred to included the financing of military units. On the first day of your examination-in-chief, you testified about how military units were organised at the municipal level and financed by municipalities. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. It was solely on that principle that the matters worked, especially in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since this problem existed of the fact that the system governing military forces was disorganized is not something that we encountered for the first time. Can you tell us now, as a member of the government, whether the decentralised system of financing helped strengthen the position of municipalities and municipal authorities in some way, in the way they were able to control the actions of local military units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just a precision, Mr. President. If we could get an idea now of the time-frame that the witness is talking about, because I personally would like to know or to be clear exactly on the time-frame that he's discussing at this point, what year, what period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm referring to the entire period. That's why I didn't specify any time-frame. I'm talking about the period in which military units were established at the level of municipalities. In the set of documents I prepared, you will find minutes from the month of October 1993, where Messrs. Stojic, Praljak and Petkovic, at a government meeting, tried to draw everybody's attention to the problem of financing military units locally, which made effective control over them impossible and created additional problems. We will come to that later, but my question right now relates to the period of 1992 and up to and until the month of October 1993. As for the rest, I will be specifying time-frames as needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, what remains in the record of your answer is: "That's true." Can you please resume giving your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For illustration's sake, I will give you an example from my personal experience. I was the commander of the defence of Citluk at the time when the municipality of Citluk was defending itself on its own. We had the Yugoslav People's Army on the southern boundaries of the municipality of Mostar and, in other words, on the northern boundaries of the municipality of Citluk. That was the situation that prevailed until the end of 1991, when due to the situation that I was faced with, that's to say, my soldiers were exhausted, there were very many wounded and the state of affairs in the units in general was very difficult, I was forced to resign. We were able to see -- and let me now be precise -- that evidence was presented before this Tribunal whereby the municipality of Ljubuski issued a decision, and this was our neighbouring southern municipality, which strictly forbade any of its soldiers to leave the municipality. So while the municipality of Citluk was bleeding to death under the burden, the adjacent municipality of Ljubuski had this decision in force which banned any of its soldiers from leaving that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, we will be talking about the decentralised system of municipalities a bit later. I would like to focus on the issue of financing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me correct an error at page 80, line 15. The year was not 1991, but 1992. We are referring to the year 1992 and 1993, up until the month of October, and the issue of financing military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, Mr. Buntic, can we conclude that there was local financing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Alaburic, I think the witness said "1991," so you should perhaps not yourself testify, but ask him whether it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm merely saying what my learned friend here wrote down for me, and I'm sure that this is true because my other colleagues were motioning to me that this was the case. But we can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It may be, Ms. Alaburic, but your learned colleague isn't the witness either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let us not waste any more time on this. We can resolve the matter in the following way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, you were telling us how you were at the Command of Citluk, and you said that this was the situation that prevailed until the end of 1991: You were faced with a situation where your soldiers were exhausted and so on and so forth. Since I really have no direct knowledge about you misspeaking or not, were you referring to 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I was merely relaying another's observation of an apparent mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to what I'm actually interested in, which is the financing of the military units in 1992 and 1993, until the month of October 1993, to be more precise. Can we conclude in a sentence whether there was local financing and whether this helped strengthen the influence of the local authorities on the leadership of the local brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure and positive that until the autumn of 1992, the municipal HVOs, in other words, the armies, were financed solely from the municipal funds. Thereafter -- well, let me tell you first that I'm not an individual who knew any of the budgetary details of the municipalities or of the HVO. I wasn't interested in that. But until the autumn of 1992, they were solely financed from municipal funds. I do not consider myself competent to speak of what the finances were like thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will be discussing that when we come to the issue of the government meetings which you, too, attended. Let me go back to a more complex set of questions which have to do with -- more directly with the defence. I see that you have received my set of documents, and I believe Their Honours have them as well. Let me just make this remark about the way the documents were sorted, and they were sorted out in the order in which I intend to put them to the witness. If I at any point decide to skip any of the documents, I will say so. The first document you have before you, Mr. Buntic, is 4D 00819, which is already in evidence. This is a Decree on the Armed Forces, the consolidated text from the month of October 1992. I'm interested in Article 9. I direct your attention to Article 9, which sets out the tasks of the Croatian Defence Council in the defence of Herceg-Bosna. It is not my intention to read all nine of the items, but I kindly ask you to cast your eye on them and tell us if, to your knowledge, these were indeed the issues that fell within the purview of the civilian HVO, that's to say, Government of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article sets out the purview. Therefore, I do confirm that this was the decree adopted on the 17th of October, 1992 -- or, rather, it wasn't passed, but it was amended and, as such, promulgated in the Official Gazette of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did the civilian HVO or, in other words, government discharge the affairs from within its purview or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it did to the extent it was able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the reports on the work of the civilian HVO, i.e., the government, contain a report on the work of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us quickly go through several minutes and other documents from the meetings of the civilian HVO, i.e., the government, which were dedicated to the military situation, political and military and security-related situation, in the territory of the HZ-HB. The first document we have in that set is one that you commented upon by saying that it was correct. That's P1227. For that reason, I will skip the document. I don't need it for my question. However, my question will have to do with the following document; namely, P1324, minutes from the meeting of the HVO on the 27th of January, 1993. You're not listed as having attended the meeting, but if you attended the following meeting, when the minutes were verified, you might be familiar with what was going on at that meeting. Did you ever see the minutes from the 27th of January, 1993, meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. As the minutes clearly show, I did not attend the meeting. I think I was abroad on business. That was the 27th of January, 1993, and I believe that my business trip lasted some 15 days, although I can't be positive about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will skip that document as well. Let's look at P1511, minutes dated the 18th of February, and you attended the meeting. Item 8 of the agenda, discussion on unauthorised mobilisation of conscripts, and a requisitioning of business premises and materiel and technical equipment from the BH Army. Tell us, Mr. Buntic, do you recall this issue being discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the document shows, I attended the meeting. However, the lapse of time took its toll. I can't remember everything that was entered into the minutes, I really cannot. But if you can jog my memory --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 8. Do you recall that part of the discussion, and do you recall anything that would be of importance to us and which would have to do with the implementation of the regulation concerning the mobilisation of conscripts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the best of will, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Document 1D 1182, 27th of February, 1993, an interim session with just one item on the agenda, "Security and military situation." It's the territory of Central Bosnia. There are a number of curious observations here, but we can focus on item 3, which says: "It is considered to be important, in order to increase the efficiency of our common struggle against the aggressor and to improve the development of Croat-Muslim relations, to form a Main Staff and to relieve of his duties Sefer Halilovic, to make changes in the Main Staff of the BH Army." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this issue was discussed, and I also remember why. There was information that the person mentioned here, a high-ranking officer of the former Counter-intelligence Service of the Yugoslav People's Army, was infiltrated as such first into the Patriotic League and then into the top echelon of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Let's move on to P1627 . It's a note from a working meeting held on 8 March 1993. I repeat the name of the -- the number of the document, P01627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is so fast, let's go back to what you have just said, Witness. If I understand properly what you said, unless I'm wrong -- if I'm wrong, please correct me straight away -- Halilovic was an officer of the Yugoslav service and who had to infiltrate the Patriotic League, and that's why he had a senior rank in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the Halilovic you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about Sefer Halilovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is this the reason why in this document it is asked that his position should be terminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, because we had information that the Counter-Intelligence Service, through its officers who had been infiltrated into the top echelon of the BH Army, is trying to provoke conflicts between Bosniaks and Croats. And to corroborate this theory of mine, I will show you a proof. I'll show you evidence from my bag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't show the evidence, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an exclusive interview given to "Slobodna Bosna" magazine by the commander of the BH Army or, rather, its first commander of the Territorial Defence, listing all the officers of the Counter-Intelligence Service of the Yugoslav Army who had, as such, been infiltrated into the top echelon of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, we were talking about document 1182. Let's move on to the next document, P1627. It's a meeting from -- it's a note from a working meeting of the 8th of March, 1993, discussing tasks for the period to follow. And in item 2(a), it states: "Establish better cooperation with military units and strengthen military commands in Central Bosnia." Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 8th of March, the spring of 1993, a time when Croat-Bosniak conflicts were already beginning in Central Bosnia. Not long after this, I visited Central Bosnia. I saw the situation with my own eyes, but I know that already then tensions were high in the area of Gornji Vakuf and in all Central Bosnia, Vitez, Busovaca, et cetera, and the first incidents were occurring between the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic, so its task in item 2(b) of this document. Let us look at another document, 1D 1664. It's a record from a HVO session of the 19th April 1993. You attended. Topic number 1 was reviewing the military and security situation in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The HVO instructs the Defence Department and the Main Staff to take all military mobilisation measures with a view to protecting Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember this order of the HVO to the Defence Department and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 19 April, when the conflict already intensified. And as we see, HVO is ordering military mobilisation measures, not specific military action but mobilisation measures; in other words, to carry out a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification. There's no dispute that the civilian HVO, that is, the government, did not issue orders for specific military operations; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was able to pass decisions and documents related to mobilisation. Every municipality could do that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Conclusion number 2 is that all the bodies and services of the HVO of HZ-HB are required to take every possible step in order to defend Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That confirms what I've said before; that is, that the first and foremost objective and the very raison d'etre of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was to defend this territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item 3 gives full support to the measures taken and the overall common action of the commands of the HVO, the military and civilian police forces, and the Main Staff of the HVO. Do you remember, was that really so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is praise given probably for the work done by then and the success achieved by then that was real.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. The next document is P2124. It's signed by Mr. Jadranko Prlic as president of the HVO. He refers to the HVO session of the 24 April 1993. And it speaks about the establishment of this working group, including you, which will visit the war-torn area and establish the state of affairs, and, depending on that, suggest specific measures to be taken. Do you remember how this working group was established?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember also that this group did accomplish its mission. We visited Central Bosnia and most of the municipalities in Central Bosnia. I have already given evidence about that, including details that we learned and that we saw during that trip across Central Bosnia. I don't think I need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No need. Let us look at the next document, 1D 1666. These are minutes of the 17 May 1993. You attended. The HVO is reviewing again the military and security situation. This time there is mention of conflicts in Mostar on the 9th of May and about an attack by Muslim forces against HVO barracks, Tihomir Misic, in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993. Do you have any knowledge about this attack on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were skirmishes in Mostar, that from the 9th of May onwards the conflict intensified. But how exactly it started, I did not have enough information about that. I didn't know anything other than what was discussed at Cabinet sessions. I had no other source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of item 1, there is mention of the HVO Commission for Exchanging Prisoners. Tell me, the HVO had such a commission back in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're about to raise a new topic. I'll go back to the 9th of May, because we have spent some hundreds of hours on the issue of the 9th of May. There is still a lot to say about this topic. Where were you on the 9th of May, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Citluk, and early in the morning I went to work from Citluk to Mostar, and I was stopped somewhere at a place we called Kobilovaca. It's a kind of pass when you start descending from Citluk towards Mostar. There were military policemen standing on the road, and I was informed that there were skirmishes in Mostar and that I shouldn't go in. They did not say, in so many words, that they forbid me to go any further, but they warned me that the conflict had escalated and that it is inadvisable to go to Mostar, after which I returned home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 8th May, again I think I was in Mostar, at work, until about 3.00 p.m. And after 3.00 p.m., I commuted every day from Mostar back home in my own car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is my third and final answer [as interpreted] to you: Had the HVO launched an attack against places held by the ABiH in Mostar? Was it within your purview to be associated with a general plan by the HVO against Muslim forces, or would you not have been involved because you were not supposed to intervene, it was not within your remit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you about an event which was typical. On that day, 9 of May, HVO arrested my deputy in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... which indicates that neither he nor I had no prior knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please indicate the name of your deputy, because it was not heard by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My deputy, Karlo Sesar, who was in the neighbouring building next to the boundary where the skirmishes were happening, in the hotbed of the conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your deputy was your right hand or was he an assistant? Was your deputy the number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was my deputy, my right hand, not assistant. In addition to him, I had two assistants, but he was not an assistant. He was a deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the HVO took him prisoner; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he was in the adjacent building, a building right on the border where the fighting was going on. And as such, he was removed from that area, from that territory. He just happened to be in the heart of the conflict. He was completely unprepared. He had no inkling of what was to come. He had no clue that a conflict could occur that day. So he was removed from that territory not in order to be arrested or detained. He was just taken away from that area from his apartment. He even lived in the next building. He lived there, resided there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Buntic, in the last paragraph of page 1, there is mention of the removal of civilians. Are you familiar with the fact that on that day, the 9th of May, 1993, the civilians who resided in the war-struck areas, those of Muslim ethnicity, had been taken away and put up for a period of some ten days to two weeks in the location of Heliodrom, and that this had been done for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my very deputy was removed -- taken out of the area where there were conflicts. I said that I was in Citluk on that day and that whatever I knew, I heard from the mass media, and I was only able to obtain official information at the next meeting of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I must say the last question that you put was not only leading, it went beyond leading, because you implied a legal qualification which you just took because it seems to suit you, as you said that they were -- they were put away for their protection. And that, I think, is not a correct way to ask the questions. You must ask whether they were taken, and then you must ask whether he knew for what purpose. That's for the next time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your guidance. Let me just tell you that I do not believe that I made a mistake. My question had to do with the third paragraph of the minutes from the government meeting, and the minutes mention the removal of the civilians. And if you look at the end of the paragraph, it says there that they were taken out of the bounds of the town for their own safety's sake. So my question related to the conclusions contained in the minutes from this government meeting, and not to any position that I may advance. I hope that this explanation satisfies your -- the issue you raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I'm certainly not accusing you of trying to play tricks. I still think that it's not a very good question, but I absolutely accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, Mr. Buntic, document 1D 1608, minutes from the HVO meeting held on the 24th of May, 1993. From the list of those in attendance, we see that you were there, but Mr. Prlic was absent. My first question is: Was this the first of the three meetings of the HVO you mentioned which Mr. Prlic did not attend after he was appointed president of the transitional government according to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that would be the first or one of the three meetings Mr. Prlic did not chair.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested, of course -- what I'm interested in, of course, is the discussion on the military and security situation.
